title: Big Data in R with Arrow
text:
Apache Arrow



Apache Arrow is a universal columnar format and multi-language toolbox for fast data interchange and in-memory analytics.



Columnar is Fast!
Arrow keeps data in a single format that can be accessed by multiple programming languages and platforms without having to copy and convert the data.
Arrow works with multiple programming languages, including C++, C#, Go, Java, Julia, Python, and of course R.

title: Big Data in R with Arrow
text: This short presentation and accompanying reference guide introduces one approach to working with larger-than-memory data analysis in R using the Apache Arrow package arrow.

title: Big Data in R with Arrow
text:
Note




Be able to explain why data analysis is faster on data organized in columns over rows.

title: Big Data in R with Arrow
text:
Apache Arrow, and the arrow package in R, is an extremely fast toolbox for larger-than-memory data analysis.

Reading and writing Apache Parquet files
Reading data in as parquet will offer a significant speedup.
If you have data loaded from csv, you can write it into a parquet file.
To load the data from a single csv, you can use open_csv_dataset("path/to/csv"), which is a wrapper to open_dataset().

taxi_data <- open_csv_dataset("data/nyc-taxi/yellow_taxi_data.csv")

To take full advantage of parquet performance you can partition your file into individual parquet files, but you must be cautious:
Partition your data into files between 20 MB and 2 GB, with no more than 10,000 partitions. Too small and reading metadata from each file will slow us down, to big and we won’t see a performance advantage over one file.
Use “hive-partitioning” when saving to split our data into multiple directories based on key variable(s) of interest In this example we will save the NYC taxi data into parquet, partitioned on the variables year and month.
Because the variables are saved in the directory names, Arrow will automatically infer the Parquet structure.

nyc_taxi |>
  write_dataset(
    "nyc-taxi/",
    format = "parquet",
    partitioning = c("year", "month"),
    hive_style = TRUE
  )

We partitioned our single csv into 196 parquet files, around 200 MB each, so we should see great performance!


When to pull data into memory
Arrow uses lazy evaluation. Your dplyr verbs aren’t executed until you explicitly tell Arrow to do so.
You can tell it two ways:
collect(): Arrow query into memory as a tibble (thousands of rows) compute(): Arrow query into memory as an Arrow Table (millions of rows)
Use nrow() liberally. This will tell you how many rows will be returned if you choose to bring the data into memory. Too many (more than a few million rows) and you likely need to filter the data down some more.

nyc_taxi |>
  filter(year %in% 2020:2026) |>
  nrow()



Schemas - here be dragons
When you read in a dataset in Arrow, it scans approximately 1 MB of the data for a csv, or the first file when reading parquet files, and guesses (imputes) the data types. If not all of your data is represented in that sample, Arrow may infer the wrong type!
Be sure to check your schema using schema(nyc_taxi). The schema() function can extract a schema from an object, but it can also be used to update a schema if yours is incorrect.


Learn more
View the arrow package documentation, or work through this excellent tutorial from posit::conf(2025).

title: Big Data in R with Arrow
text:
Lazy Evaluation
While our dplyr verbs will feel familiar in Arrow, there is a subtle difference in how the code is evaluated. Normally, in dplyr, everything is run and a data frame (or tibble, depending on your input) is returned.
When you know that the result of your dplyr query will be larger than your available memory, that could be dangerous. That’s why Arrow uses lazy evaluation. Your dplyr verbs aren’t executed until you explicitly tell Arrow to do so.
You can tell it two ways:
compute(): bring the results of the Arrow query into memory as an Arrow Table collect(): bring the results of the Arrow query into memory as a tibble

title: Big Data in R with Arrow
text:
Arrow vs Dataset
Picking the right tool for job.
Larger than Memory: Dataset: When the data won’t fit into memory.
Smaller than Memory Millions of rows: Arrow Thousands of rows (or less): Tibble

Rule of thumb
If you know the data is larger than your memory, start with a Dataset.
Use nrow() liberally to understand how many rows would be returned by a query. If in the millions, stick with Arrow. If thousands or less, go with tibble.

title: Big Data in R with Arrow
text:
dplyr query

Calculate the percent of rides that are shared by year


library(dplyr)
nyc_taxi |>                                                        
  group_by(year) |> 
  summarize(
    total_rides = n(), 
    shared_rides = sum(passenger_count > 1,
                       na.rm = TRUE)
    ) |> 
  mutate(percent_shared = (shared_rides / total_rides) * 100)

FileSystemDataset (query)
year: int64
total_rides: int64
shared_rides: uint64
percent_shared: double (multiply_checked(divide(cast(shared_rides, {to_type=double, allow_int_overflow=false, allow_time_truncate=false, allow_time_overflow=false, allow_decimal_truncate=false, allow_float_truncate=false, allow_invalid_utf8=false}), cast(total_rides, {to_type=double, allow_int_overflow=false, allow_time_truncate=false, allow_time_overflow=false, allow_decimal_truncate=false, allow_float_truncate=false, allow_invalid_utf8=false})), 100))

title: Big Data in R with Arrow
text:
Summary - that was alot
The arrow package is an implementation of Apache Arrow in R. . . .
It allows fast data analysis of larger-than-memory data in R using standard dplyr verbs.

Some key takeaways:

If you have big data, load it into an Arrow Dataset with open_dataset().
Most dplyr verbs work, just don’t forget to bring the result into memory.

Thousands of rows? Use collect() to a tibble
Millions of rows? Use compute() to an Arrow Table

If you are working with big data, generally you should read/write in Parquet. ::: incremental
